name: Cold water rinse

lead: A cold water rinse means finishing a hair wash with cool or cold water. People who do it say it leaves hair shinier and smoother.
The idea rests on the belief that cold water closes the cuticle. No studies of the practice on hair were found.

paras: The practice is a final rinse at lower temperature. The proposed explanation is that the outer cuticle scales lie flatter, reflecting more light.
No documented harms specific to the practice were found. Cold exposure itself may be uncomfortable for some people.

lead: A cold water rinse is a hair-care habit of finishing a wash with cool or cold water. Proponents say it makes hair look shinier and smoother, with the reasoning that cold water closes or flattens the hair cuticle.

Wikipedia's article on hair care describes the cuticle as part of a shaft with no living processes, so care focuses on keeping it intact, and notes that chemical processing can leave the cuticle unable to close fully [1]. The article does not discuss water temperature, and no published studies of cold water rinses on hair shine or smoothness were found.

paras: The practice consists of ending a shower or wash with a final rinse of cold or cool water instead of warm water. It requires no product.

Proponents describe the cold finish as sealing the cuticle so that light reflects more evenly. Wikipedia notes that the cuticle is the outer layer of the hair shaft and that damage to the visible shaft cannot be repaired by a biological process [1]. It also reports that acidic shampoos in the pH 4 to 6 range are the most common type because they do not swell the hair shaft [1]. Those sources describe cuticle behaviour and shampoo pH but do not test water temperature.
No studies found. No human or laboratory studies of cold water rinses on hair shine, smoothness or cuticle position were located.
